passages.label: A
passages.text: Since 1993, satellites have measured sea level across much of the ocean. Combining separate passes into a comparable record is a challenge because instruments and sea conditions change. Scientists therefore calibrate measurements and compare records from satellites with observations from coastal tide gauges. Individual annual values may rise or fall, while a longer trend can reveal a persistent change that short-term fluctuations hide. At a coast, a local record can help make sense of the readings from space.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A record of rising sea level points to physical changes in both the ocean and the land. Warmer seawater occupies more space through thermal expansion, while melting glaciers and ice sheets contribute more water, the two mechanisms NASA identifies as the principal contributors to recent global sea-level rise. Their combined effect connects increasing global temperatures with higher mean sea level over time, even though a record of the global average cannot tell an observer what happened during a particular tide or storm.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Satellite observations also reveal seasonal fluctuations in the height of the ocean. Water circulates between the sea and the land through precipitation such as rain and snow, which can temporarily raise or lower the measured global level. To distinguish recurrent seasonal variation from a change that continues for decades, researchers compare multiple years of observations. A storm can produce a marked change in water height at one coast. But that local event alone cannot establish the direction in which global sea level is moving. A satellite record can reveal changes in regional circulation, but interpreting the distribution of those changes requires additional evidence, especially where seasonal variation obscures a longer-term signal. An observation system can provide evidence about the risk of a coastal disaster. A long-term trend can also show an environmental change. The benefit of readings from space is wide coverage, while a local alternative is valuable where other measurements are limited.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Sea-level records form one part of the wider evidence for climate change. The atmosphere contains gases including carbon dioxide and methane that trap heat, and burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas releases additional carbon dioxide. NASA explains that the concentration of this gas has increased as a result of human activity since the industrial era. A satellite designed for measuring ocean height serves a different purpose from an instrument that measures atmospheric gases, yet both kinds of observation contribute to understanding the climate system.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Satellites help with a global issue, whereas coastal observations help predict what could happen along one shore. An ocean that absorbs more heat as a result of global warming expands and raises sea level, yet local variations can also reflect land movement, circulation and temporary surges. A greenhouse gas released when a fossil fuel is burned can contribute to this warming through its effect on the atmosphere. The consequences can threaten a coastal ecosystem or complicate plans for new construction, particularly where roads and buildings sit close to the current water level.

R_H2.passageTitle: Why the Ocean Takes Up Heat

passages.label: A
passages.text: Within the climate system, the ocean acts as a reservoir for much of the extra heat that accumulates as greenhouse gases alter Earth's energy balance. This uptake can moderate the immediate rise of air temperature, even as the energy absorbed affects the ocean itself. Researchers therefore compare changes in the atmosphere with observations of how heat is distributed in marine environments, and an assessment confined to air temperature could overlook changes occurring at different depths beneath the ocean surface.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, where the gas contributes to heat retention. The ocean also absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide, linking conditions in the air to changes in seawater through a mechanism distinct from the transfer of heat. Neither process means that the ocean can continue absorbing unlimited amounts without consequences.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Warming water has a physical result. Like many materials, seawater expands as it becomes warmer, and this expansion contributes to rising global sea level, alongside water added by melting land ice, and the ocean’s heat uptake is therefore not simply a helpful service. It is also part of the evidence used to understand global warming, and a measurement of one process can lead to questions about another process, but scientists still need a number of kinds of observations. When researchers compare data from two places, they need to check how deep the instruments were and when they took their readings. Some areas warm faster than others. A reading from one place also cannot tell us what changed elsewhere, and an observation system can provide evidence about the long-term risk to an environmental resource such as a reef. Combining measurements from different depths offers a benefit where surface observations are limited. An alternative record is useful when instruments are moved. Such changes are an issue when comparing different stations.

passages.label: D
passages.text: As NOAA explains, carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater changes its chemistry, making the water more acidic and altering conditions for organisms that use dissolved materials to build shells or skeletons. Other inhabitants of a marine ecosystem can be affected indirectly when food or shelter depends on organisms that respond to the chemical change. The magnitude of these effects can vary with the species and habitat, so a general account of acidification cannot establish exactly what every organism will experience.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A reef image illustrates the difference between detecting an effect and identifying its cause. NASA’s pictures of a reef in American Samoa in 2014 and 2015 document a change, but establishing an annual trend or predicting consequences for another ecosystem requires a longer record. Measurements of temperature, depth and the timing of local disturbances help researchers decide which explanations remain plausible. Carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas released when a fossil fuel is burned, contributes to global warming, which can threaten marine life, while the ocean can also absorb carbon dioxide and change in chemical ways. Treating these pressures separately allows comparisons across locations without implying that the same process accounts for every observation.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A satellite image can map the disappearance of tree cover without identifying the underlying drivers. The Food and Agriculture Organization distinguishes deforestation, the permanent conversion of a forest to another land use, from degradation, a decline in the quality of a forest that remains in place. Loss of cover and loss of ecological function may interact. But the terms identify different kinds of change.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Direct drivers include commercial and local agriculture, infrastructure expansion, mining and urban growth, which can change what people do with the land around a forest. Replacing a bridge on an existing road may extend access less than a new road into terrain previously inaccessible to heavy vehicles. If new access reduces transport costs, growing crops can become more profitable even though the work in the fields remains equally demanding. Researchers must establish whether that mechanism operated in the particular location, since the same consequences cannot be assumed for every road.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Forest ecosystems store carbon, sustain biodiversity and regulate water, but many rainforest species depend on connected habitats that roads can fragment by opening previously inaccessible land. Logging can be followed by the recovery of forest cover, whereas permanent conversion removes that possibility as long as the new land use continues. Two plots may support the same number of species and regulate water similarly, yet measurements of biomass may reveal substantial differences in the amount of carbon that remains stored after mature trees have been removed. A comparison of one function therefore cannot describe all the ecological consequences of forest loss.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Underlying influences include markets, laws, land rights, poverty, technology and government decisions, which operate at global, national and local levels. A wealthier person may still have less authority to approve a change because they have weaker land rights. In two otherwise comparable areas, poverty can restrict the money available to pay for alternatives to clearing, while an international change in product prices may outweigh a decision made within the affected community. The FAO therefore recommends location-specific assessment that combines recent monitoring, historical information, local knowledge and relevant reports, because a general observation about agriculture may suggest a plausible cause without establishing whether it affected a particular forest. Evidence about a forest resource can provide a basis for an affordable alternative to clearing the land. Its long-term benefit may depend on the risk of environmental change and on whether a proposed solution works where other choices are limited.

passages.label: E
passages.text: As trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the destruction of a rainforest changes both carbon storage and conditions within the ecosystem. More carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, can contribute to global warming, although these consequences do not establish which activity cleared a particular place. If farming is the main cause, policies can address agricultural land use and demand for food, whereas a measure designed only around farms may have little effect where road construction encouraged logging. To predict what a policy can achieve, compare the cause it targets with evidence from the locations it is supposed to protect.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Two wooded areas lose the same amount of tree cover. One remains forest and loses quality, and the other becomes permanent farmland. How would the article classify them?
options: Both are deforestation as long as the image looks the same.
Both are degradation because the land had trees before.
The first is degradation and the second is deforestation.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a new route have a different impact from repairing a crossing on an old one?
options: Repairing any crossing changes farming costs by the same amount everywhere.
A new route can open land that heavy vehicles previously could not reach.
A new route has an effect only if it makes work in the fields easier.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could better access change the economic result from growing crops even if the work is unchanged?
options: Moving goods can cost less, making crops more profitable.
Growers would have to pay more to get goods out, so profits would necessarily rise.
Growers would lose their ability to sell whenever a road was available.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can two areas with similar tree cover still raise different concerns for conservation?
options: Once tree cover matches, the two areas are classed as having the same quality by definition.
Matching cover determines exactly how much carbon is held in each area.
Cover alone may give the same impression while other evidence, such as differences in stored carbon, tells a different story.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: When can a previously logged site regain forest cover in the example?
options: Recovery is possible where the area has not been permanently kept for another use.
The chances are greatest if permanent use as a farm continues.
The article says cover cannot return after any trees have been logged.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why might a person with more money lack the power to approve a land-use change?
options: Everyone with more money automatically has more authority over land.
Their rights over the land may be weaker.
Authority depends only on how long the trees have been growing.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A report blames farming for a forest loss because it is a common cause in the country. What further work would justify making that claim at this site?
options: Confirm only that people somewhere in the country grow the same crop.
Count the total number of roads in the country without asking how the forest was used.
Use past and current local evidence to check whether farming actually explains the loss and whether other influences mattered.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A survey estimates how much carbon was lost when a forest was cleared. What would still need other evidence about the site?
options: Which activity caused the trees to be cleared
Whether the survey expressed the loss as an amount of carbon
Whether the survey recorded a consequence of the clearing

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would be a weakness in a policy aimed only at changing how farms use land?
options: It would always make the effect of every new road easier to predict.
It could miss the main problem in an area where road building promoted logging.
It could never help any area where most trees are cleared for agriculture.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which argument best fits the whole article's reasoning about forest loss?
options: An image of missing trees establishes the cause, the quality of the remaining forest and the best policy in every case.
If two forests provide the same water benefits, a change to either is guaranteed to have the same overall effect.
Establish the kind and extent of the change, verify the causes at that location and test whether a policy addresses them.
